VIDEO.title: Matthew 10:1-15 – The Ancient Gospel Message You Never Knew About!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 10:1-15: Jesus summons the Twelve, gives them authority over unclean spirits and disease, names them, and sends them out with instructions. This begins His second great discourse in Matthew, the 'mission' discourse, which runs to the end of chapter 10.

In verse 1 they are 'disciples'; in verse 2, for the only time in Matthew, they are 'apostles.' An apostle is 'one who is sent,' an authorized representative. A disciple (talmid) is being trained to be like his rabbi. Peter is named first: first among the Twelve in leadership, as Acts shows.

How could they preach good news before the cross? Their message was 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand' (10:7), and every phrase comes out of the Old Testament: 'lost sheep' (Psalm 119:176; Jeremiah 50:6; Ezekiel 34), the King installed on Zion (Psalm 2), the Son of Man given an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14), and the righteous Branch of David (Jeremiah 23:5-6). The good news was that the King had arrived.

'Freely you received, freely give' (10:8) echoes Isaiah 55:1: buy wine and milk 'without money and without cost,' leading to an everlasting covenant and the faithful lovingkindnesses of David. No money and no moral resume can buy entry to God's banquet; the only requirement is to listen and believe.

So they take almost nothing, rely on God's provision, look for whoever is 'worthy' in each town, and stay there. A house that rejects them gets the dust shaken off their feet, and that town will fare worse than Sodom and Gomorrah.

The lesson: when God sends His people on a mission, He gives them everything they need to accomplish it, even the people who need to hear. Like the Son, we do what we see the Father doing (John 5:19).
QUOTES: The word apostle means one who is sent.
The good news was simply to proclaim that the king had arrived.
Their job is to go looking for those people who are already worthy.
When God sends his people on a mission, he gives them everything they need to accomplish it.
This is the way to do ministry, ladies and gentlemen, to recognize what the Father is already doing and just go be a part of it.

method.p: The teacher's tip: Jesus' words are full of the Old Testament, and he has not shown you every link. Keep looking: he points to 1 Samuel 25, Nehemiah 5 and Genesis 19 and leaves them for you to find.

LSB_QUOTES.text: And you who have no money come, buy and eat. Come, buy wine and milk / Without money and without cost.
And as you go, preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’

src.text: And summoning His twelve disciples, Jesus gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every kind of disease and every kind of sickness. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; and James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;

lines.text: Verse 1 says 'disciples'; verse 2 says 'apostles,' the only time Matthew uses the word. An apostle is one who is sent: an emissary or ambassador who acts as an authorized representative.
The stages of their training: first they watch Jesus teach and heal; then they help their rabbi; now they are sent out, to report back later; finally, after the ascension, they spread His church.
Matthew does not narrate their trip or return. Mark and Luke do: 'the apostles gathered together with Jesus; and they reported to Him all that they had done and taught' (Mark 6:30).

src.text: Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; and James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;

lines.text: Peter is first, not because he was called first, but because he leads the Twelve. Acts shows it: Peter preaches and performs miracles in its first half. Some scholars call him 'first among equals' (primus inter pares).
Every list of the Twelve puts Peter first and Judas Iscariot last (Mark 3:16-19; Luke 6:14-16; Acts 1:13).

src.text: Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed Him.

lines.text: Matthew lists the Twelve in pairs; perhaps the very pairs that went out. Mark says Jesus sent them out 'in pairs' (Mark 6:7).
Thaddaeus is likely the second Judas of the Twelve: Luke and Acts list 'Judas the son of James,' and John mentions 'Judas (not Iscariot).'
Matthew calls himself 'the tax collector' (10:3), the only list that does.

src.text: These twelve Jesus sent out after instructing them, saying, “Do not go in the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter any city of the Samaritans; but rather go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

lines.text: In practice: do not head north toward Tyre and Sidon, east toward the Decapolis, or south into the Samaritan towns. Stay in Galilee and minister to the Jews.
Jesus says the same of His own mission in 15:24. After the resurrection He sends them to 'all the nations' (28:19).

left.text: I have wandered off like a lost sheep; search for Your slave, / For I have not forgotten Your commandments.

right.text: “My people have become lost sheep; / Their shepherds have led them astray. / They have made them turn away on the mountains;

lines.text: The psalmist knows God but has lost his way. Jesus is telling the apostles to look for that kind of person.
Jeremiah blames the shepherds: the religious leaders who failed to lead the flock. Ezekiel 34 says the same, and God promises to gather His sheep Himself.

MESSAGE.kicker: The kingdom is at hand · Psalm 2
MESSAGE.title: My King upon Zion

src.text: “But as for Me, I have installed My King / Upon Zion, My holy mountain.” “I will surely tell of the decree of Yahweh: / He said to Me, ‘You are My Son, / Today I have begotten You.

lines.text: How could they preach good news before the cross and resurrection? Their message was the kingdom (10:7). Psalm 2 looks to the great King on Zion, given the nations and the ends of the earth.
The good news before the cross was that the King had arrived. Afterward the resurrection became the proof that He is who He claimed to be.

MESSAGE.title: One like a Son of Man

src.text: And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed.

lines.text: The video links Psalm 2 to Daniel 7: the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom that will never pass away.
Jesus calls Himself the Son of Man (8:20; 9:6), and at His trial quotes Daniel 7:13 (26:64).

src.text: “Behold, the days are coming,” declares Yahweh, / “When I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; / And He will reign as king and prosper / And do justice and righteousness in the land.

lines.text: His name will be 'Yahweh our righteousness' (Jeremiah 23:6). All this is backdrop for what the apostles were to tell the towns: lost sheep, the kingdom, the King. Jesus gave them a solid biblical basis for their claims.
The signs go with the message: heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons (10:8). Jews who knew their Tanakh should have understood what these meant.

left.text: Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you received, freely give.

right.text: “Ho! Every one who thirsts, come to the waters; / And you who have no money come, buy and eat. / Come, buy wine and milk / Without money and without cost.

lines.text: Why jump from good news to money? The video says Jesus is drawing on Isaiah 55: come and buy what is actually free. It leads straight to an everlasting covenant 'according to the faithful lovingkindnesses of David' (55:3), a nod to David's throne.

No money and no righteous deed can buy a place at God's royal banquet, yet He invites His people anyway. So the apostles must be radically generous with the message. The only requirement is that people listen and believe.

src.text: “For a brief moment I forsook you, / But with great compassion I will gather you. In a flood of fury / I hid My face from you for a moment, / But with everlasting lovingkindness I will have compassion on you,” / Says Yahweh your Redeemer.

lines.text: Isaiah 55 follows the suffering Servant of chapter 53, who 'interceded for the transgressors' (53:12), and the covenant of peace in chapter 54.
Compassion links it all: Jesus saw shepherdless sheep and felt compassion (9:36); the Lord's compassion moves Him to redeem and bless His people.

FREELY.title: The worker is worthy of his support

src.text: Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your money belts, or a bag for your journey, or even two tunics, or sandals, or a staff; for the worker is worthy of his support. And whatever city or village you enter, inquire who is worthy in it, and stay there until you leave.

lines.text: Taking almost nothing forced them to shun luxury and rely on God's provision. They do not need a resume-ready audience; they only need people willing to listen.
'Inquire who is worthy': the video reads it as God having already prepared people to hear. Their job is not to make anyone worthy but to find those who are.
Paul quotes Jesus' saying as Scripture: 'The laborer is worthy of his wages' (1 Timothy 5:18; Luke 10:7).

FREELY.title: Shake the dust off your feet

src.text: And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it. But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. And whoever does not receive you, nor heed your words, as you leave that house or that city, shake the dust off your feet.

lines.text: Jesus does not tell them to win whole towns: they find individual houses, and a house that rejects them stands for the town. The video explains the dust as a Jewish custom on leaving Gentile land, so it marks the town as no different from the pagans.

The connections the teacher leaves for you: David's greeting 'peace be to your house' (1 Samuel 25:6); Nehemiah shaking out his garment as a sign against those who break their word (Nehemiah 5:13); and Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24-25).
Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch: 'having shaken off the dust of their feet against them, they went to Iconium' (Acts 13:51).

TERMS.def: Greek apostolos, 'one who is sent': an authorized representative. Matthew uses it only in 10:2.
Hebrew for a disciple: one being trained to be like his rabbi.
Latin, 'first among equals': how some scholars describe Peter among the Twelve.
Matthew 10, the mission discourse: the second of Jesus' five long teachings in Matthew (after the Sermon on the Mount).
Matthew's usual phrase for God's kingdom: the reign of the promised King, now 'at hand.'
God's people strayed or scattered (Psalm 119:176; Jeremiah 50:6).
A title for David's promised heir (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15; Zechariah 3:8).
A sign of leaving a place that rejected the message: 'a testimony against them' (Mark 6:11).

WORDS.gloss: One sent; messenger, apostle. Look up: BDAG, ἀπόστολος.
To destroy; to lose; middle: be lost.
As a gift, without payment; 'freely.' Look up: BDAG, δωρεάν.
Peace; the greeting of peace (Hebrew shalom).
To perish; to be lost or strayed. Look up: BDB or HALOT, אָבַד.

BACKGROUND.p: Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five long discourses, each closing with a line like 'when Jesus had finished' (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Many readers compare the five to the five books of Moses.

Galilee was Jewish country ringed by others: Phoenician Tyre and Sidon to the north, the Greek cities of the Decapolis to the east, and Samaria to the south, whose people worshiped at Mount Gerizim (John 4:20).
A traveler normally carried a staff, a bag for food, coins in a belt, and a spare tunic. The Twelve were to go without and depend on the hospitality of the worthy.

BACKGROUND.h: Hospitality and the greeting of peace
BACKGROUND.p: A guest greeted a household with 'peace' (shalom), as David's men did (1 Samuel 25:6). Receiving the messenger meant receiving the one who sent him (10:40).

WITNESSES.text: See how He provides for their conduct, and that no less than for their miracles, implying that the miracles without this are nothing.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 32, on 10:8. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: But what means, Shake off the dust of your feet? It is either to signify their having received nothing of them, or to be a witness to them of the long journey, which they had travelled for their sake.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 32, on 10:14. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Let every apostle that comes to you be received as the Lord. ... And when the apostle goes away, let him take nothing but bread until he lodges; but if he ask money, he is a false prophet.
WITNESSES.src: Didache 11, an early Christian church manual. Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The video: people God has already prepared to hear. Chrysostom: a fit host who will feed them and whom they need not leave for a better house. Both readings keep the burden off the messengers.

Matthew and Luke say take no staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3); Mark says 'except a staff only' (Mark 6:8). Matthew's verb is 'acquire': do not get extra gear for the trip. Readers explain the difference in several ways.
The video: it treats the town like Gentile land. Chrysostom: a sign they took nothing from it, or a witness of the long journey made for its sake. Mark and Luke call it 'a testimony against them.'
This mission was to Israel (10:5-6; 15:24). After the resurrection the commission goes to all nations (28:19). Matthew holds both: Israel first, then the world.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Jews shook Gentile dust off their feet when returning home. Commentaries often say this, but the Gospels do not explain the gesture beyond 'a testimony against them' (Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5), so hold that background loosely.
Five discourses do structure Matthew, but the link to the five books of the Torah is an interpretation; Matthew never states it, and 'every good Jew would have recognized' it cannot be shown.
The quotation from Gary Smith's New American Commentary on Isaiah could not be checked here; read it in the commentary itself before repeating it.

The link from 'freely give' to Isaiah 55 is the video's reading: Isaiah speaks of buying 'without money and without cost,' while Jesus speaks of receiving and giving 'freely.' The idea fits; the wording is not a quotation.
The video reads from another English translation ('You received without paying, give without pay'); the LSB has 'Freely you received, freely give' (10:8).

QUESTIONS: What is the difference between a disciple and an apostle? Which describes where you are right now?
If you had only the Old Testament, how would you explain 'the kingdom of heaven is at hand'?
Which of the passages (Psalm 2, Daniel 7, Jeremiah 23, Isaiah 55) helps you most to see Jesus as King?
What have you 'freely received'? Where is God asking you to give freely?
Do you ever trust yourself to accomplish God's mission instead of the God who sent you?
Where do you see the Father already at work around you this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: when God sends His people on a mission, He gives them everything they need to accomplish it. Not only food, supplies and shelter, but the very people who need to hear the message: 'inquire who is worthy.' The apostles did not have to make anyone worthy by their own great efforts; their job was to find those God had already prepared. The lesson is the same for us: if God sends us on a mission, He will give us everything we need. Sometimes we do not understand the mission in the moment, and sometimes we trust ourselves instead of the God who sent us. Jesus said, 'the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing' (John 5:19). This is the way to do ministry: recognize what the Father is already doing and go be a part of it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before you plan your next act of service, pray through Matthew 10:7-8. Write down one place you see the Father already at work (a person, a need, an open door), and one thing you have freely received that you can freely give there this week.

## Disciples become apostles
1. Disciples, then apostles · Matthew 10:1-2: One who is sent
   Apostle Matthew 10:1-2: "And summoning His twelve disciples, Jesus gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every kind of disease and every kind of sickness. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; and James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:1-2
   (video) Verse 1 says 'disciples'; verse 2 says 'apostles,' the only time Matthew uses the word. An apostle is one who is sent: an emissary or ambassador who acts as an authorized representative.
   (video) The stages of their training: first they watch Jesus teach and heal; then they help their rabbi; now they are sent out, to report back later; finally, after the ascension, they spread His church. (Mark 6:30; Luke 9:10)
   [Background] Matthew does not narrate their trip or return. Mark and Luke do: 'the apostles gathered together with Jesus; and they reported to Him all that they had done and taught' (Mark 6:30).
2. The first · Matthew 10:2: Simon, who is called Peter
   First Matthew 10:2: "Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; and James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:2
   (video) Peter is first, not because he was called first, but because he leads the Twelve. Acts shows it: Peter preaches and performs miracles in its first half. Some scholars call him 'first among equals' (primus inter pares). (Acts 2:14; Acts 3:6)
   [Background] Every list of the Twelve puts Peter first and Judas Iscariot last (Mark 3:16-19; Luke 6:14-16; Acts 1:13). (Mark 3:16-19; Luke 6:14-16)
3. Two by two · Matthew 10:2-4: Named in pairs
   Pairs Matthew 10:3-4: "Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed Him." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:3-4
   (video) Matthew lists the Twelve in pairs; perhaps the very pairs that went out. Mark says Jesus sent them out 'in pairs' (Mark 6:7). (Mark 6:7)
   (video) Thaddaeus is likely the second Judas of the Twelve: Luke and Acts list 'Judas the son of James,' and John mentions 'Judas (not Iscariot).' (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13; John 14:22)
   [Background] Matthew calls himself 'the tax collector' (10:3), the only list that does.
4. Where to go · Matthew 10:5-6: The lost sheep of Israel
   Israel first Matthew 10:5-6: "These twelve Jesus sent out after instructing them, saying, “Do not go in the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter any city of the Samaritans; but rather go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:5-6
   (video) In practice: do not head north toward Tyre and Sidon, east toward the Decapolis, or south into the Samaritan towns. Stay in Galilee and minister to the Jews.
   [Background] Jesus says the same of His own mission in 15:24. After the resurrection He sends them to 'all the nations' (28:19). (Matthew 15:24; Matthew 28:19)

## Good news before the cross
1. Lost sheep · Psalm 119 and Jeremiah 50: Who to look for
   The psalmist (Psalm 119:176, LSB): "I have wandered off like a lost sheep; search for Your slave, / For I have not forgotten Your commandments."
   Jeremiah (Jeremiah 50:6, LSB): "“My people have become lost sheep; / Their shepherds have led them astray. / They have made them turn away on the mountains;"
   (video) The psalmist knows God but has lost his way. Jesus is telling the apostles to look for that kind of person.
   (video) Jeremiah blames the shepherds: the religious leaders who failed to lead the flock. Ezekiel 34 says the same, and God promises to gather His sheep Himself. (Ezekiel 34:11-12)
2. The kingdom is at hand · Psalm 2: My King upon Zion
   The King Psalm 2:6-7: "“But as for Me, I have installed My King / Upon Zion, My holy mountain.” “I will surely tell of the decree of Yahweh: / He said to Me, ‘You are My Son, / Today I have begotten You." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Psalm+2:6-7
   (video) How could they preach good news before the cross and resurrection? Their message was the kingdom (10:7). Psalm 2 looks to the great King on Zion, given the nations and the ends of the earth. (Psalm 2:8)
   (video) The good news before the cross was that the King had arrived. Afterward the resurrection became the proof that He is who He claimed to be.
3. Daniel 7:13-14: One like a Son of Man
   Dominion Daniel 7:14: "And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Daniel+7:14
   (video) The video links Psalm 2 to Daniel 7: the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom that will never pass away. (Daniel 7:13)
   [Background] Jesus calls Himself the Son of Man (8:20; 9:6), and at His trial quotes Daniel 7:13 (26:64). (Matthew 26:64)
4. Jeremiah 23:5-6: A righteous Branch for David
   Branch Jeremiah 23:5: "“Behold, the days are coming,” declares Yahweh, / “When I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; / And He will reign as king and prosper / And do justice and righteousness in the land." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Jeremiah+23:5
   (video) His name will be 'Yahweh our righteousness' (Jeremiah 23:6). All this is backdrop for what the apostles were to tell the towns: lost sheep, the kingdom, the King. Jesus gave them a solid biblical basis for their claims. (Jeremiah 23:6)
   (video) The signs go with the message: heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons (10:8). Jews who knew their Tanakh should have understood what these meant. (Isaiah 35:5-6)

## Freely you received
1. Freely · Matthew 10:8 and Isaiah 55: Without money and without cost
   Jesus (Matthew 10:8, LSB): "Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you received, freely give."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 55:1, LSB): "“Ho! Every one who thirsts, come to the waters; / And you who have no money come, buy and eat. / Come, buy wine and milk / Without money and without cost."
   (video) Why jump from good news to money? The video says Jesus is drawing on Isaiah 55: come and buy what is actually free. It leads straight to an everlasting covenant 'according to the faithful lovingkindnesses of David' (55:3), a nod to David's throne. (Isaiah 55:3)
   (video) No money and no righteous deed can buy a place at God's royal banquet, yet He invites His people anyway. So the apostles must be radically generous with the message. The only requirement is that people listen and believe.
2. Isaiah 53-55: With great compassion
   Compassion Isaiah 54:7-8: "“For a brief moment I forsook you, / But with great compassion I will gather you. In a flood of fury / I hid My face from you for a moment, / But with everlasting lovingkindness I will have compassion on you,” / Says Yahweh your Redeemer." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+54:7-8
   (video) Isaiah 55 follows the suffering Servant of chapter 53, who 'interceded for the transgressors' (53:12), and the covenant of peace in chapter 54. (Isaiah 53:12; Isaiah 54:10)
   (video) Compassion links it all: Jesus saw shepherdless sheep and felt compassion (9:36); the Lord's compassion moves Him to redeem and bless His people. (Matthew 9:36)
3. Take nothing · Matthew 10:9-11: The worker is worthy of his support
   Provision Matthew 10:9-11: "Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your money belts, or a bag for your journey, or even two tunics, or sandals, or a staff; for the worker is worthy of his support. And whatever city or village you enter, inquire who is worthy in it, and stay there until you leave." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:9-11
   (video) Taking almost nothing forced them to shun luxury and rely on God's provision. They do not need a resume-ready audience; they only need people willing to listen.
   (video) 'Inquire who is worthy': the video reads it as God having already prepared people to hear. Their job is not to make anyone worthy but to find those who are.
   [Background] Paul quotes Jesus' saying as Scripture: 'The laborer is worthy of his wages' (1 Timothy 5:18; Luke 10:7). (1 Timothy 5:18; Luke 10:7)
4. Peace or dust · Matthew 10:12-15: Shake the dust off your feet
   Testimony Matthew 10:13-14: "And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it. But if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. And whoever does not receive you, nor heed your words, as you leave that house or that city, shake the dust off your feet." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:13-14
   (video) Jesus does not tell them to win whole towns: they find individual houses, and a house that rejects them stands for the town. The video explains the dust as a Jewish custom on leaving Gentile land, so it marks the town as no different from the pagans.
   [Background] The connections the teacher leaves for you: David's greeting 'peace be to your house' (1 Samuel 25:6); Nehemiah shaking out his garment as a sign against those who break their word (Nehemiah 5:13); and Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24-25). (1 Samuel 25:6; Nehemiah 5:13; Genesis 19:24-25)
   [Background] Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch: 'having shaken off the dust of their feet against them, they went to Iconium' (Acts 13:51). (Acts 13:51)

## Key people
- Jesus: Gives the Twelve authority, names them, and sends them with a message rooted in the Old Testament. [Background] This is the second of five long discourses in Matthew (chapters 5-7, 10, 13, 18, 24-25).
- The Twelve apostles: Disciples now sent as authorized representatives, two by two. [Background] Their names also appear in Mark 3:16-19, Luke 6:14-16 and Acts 1:13.
- Simon Peter: Named first: first among equals in leadership. [Background] Matthew alone adds 'The first' to his name in the list.
- Matthew the tax collector: Read in the list of names. [Background] Only Matthew's own list calls him 'the tax collector' (10:3); compare his call in 9:9.
- Thaddaeus: Likely the second Judas among the Twelve. [Background] Luke and Acts name 'Judas the son of James'; John 14:22 has 'Judas (not Iscariot).'
- Judas Iscariot: Named last: 'the one who betrayed Him.' [Background] He is last in every list of the Twelve.
- The Samaritans: Their towns were off-limits for this mission. [Background] Later Jesus sends His witnesses to 'Judea and Samaria' (Acts 1:8).
- Nehemiah: One of the Old Testament connections to find. [Background] He shook out his garment against anyone who broke the oath to free their brothers from debt.

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' base in Galilee, from which the Twelve were likely sent.
- Tyre (named in the video): North: a Gentile city on the coast. The video: avoid going north toward Tyre and Sidon.
- Hippos: A Decapolis city across the lake.
- Gerasa: A large Decapolis city east of the Jordan.
- Samaria (Sebaste): South: the Samaritan heartland. 'Do not enter any city of the Samaritans.'
- Nazareth: One of the Galilean towns of the lost sheep of Israel.

## Key terms
- Apostle: Greek apostolos, 'one who is sent': an authorized representative. Matthew uses it only in 10:2.
- Talmid: Hebrew for a disciple: one being trained to be like his rabbi.
- Primus inter pares: Latin, 'first among equals': how some scholars describe Peter among the Twelve.
- Second discourse: Matthew 10, the mission discourse: the second of Jesus' five long teachings in Matthew (after the Sermon on the Mount).
- Kingdom of heaven: Matthew's usual phrase for God's kingdom: the reign of the promised King, now 'at hand.'
- Lost sheep: God's people strayed or scattered (Psalm 119:176; Jeremiah 50:6).
- Branch: A title for David's promised heir (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15; Zechariah 3:8). [Background]
- Shaking off the dust: A sign of leaving a place that rejected the message: 'a testimony against them' (Mark 6:11).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Five discourses: Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five long discourses, each closing with a line like 'when Jesus had finished' (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Many readers compare the five to the five books of Moses.
- Galilee and its neighbors: Galilee was Jewish country ringed by others: Phoenician Tyre and Sidon to the north, the Greek cities of the Decapolis to the east, and Samaria to the south, whose people worshiped at Mount Gerizim (John 4:20).
- Traveling light: A traveler normally carried a staff, a bag for food, coins in a belt, and a spare tunic. The Twelve were to go without and depend on the hospitality of the worthy.
- Hospitality and the greeting of peace: A guest greeted a household with 'peace' (shalom), as David's men did (1 Samuel 25:6). Receiving the messenger meant receiving the one who sent him (10:40).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "See how He provides for their conduct, and that no less than for their miracles, implying that the miracles without this are nothing." Homilies on Matthew 32, on 10:8. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "But what means, Shake off the dust of your feet? It is either to signify their having received nothing of them, or to be a witness to them of the long journey, which they had travelled for their sake." Homilies on Matthew 32, on 10:14. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- The Didache (c. AD 50-120): "Let every apostle that comes to you be received as the Lord. ... And when the apostle goes away, let him take nothing but bread until he lodges; but if he ask money, he is a false prophet." Didache 11, an early Christian church manual. Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 7 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Who is 'worthy'? The video: people God has already prepared to hear. Chrysostom: a fit host who will feed them and whom they need not leave for a better house. Both readings keep the burden off the messengers.
- A staff or no staff? Matthew and Luke say take no staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3); Mark says 'except a staff only' (Mark 6:8). Matthew's verb is 'acquire': do not get extra gear for the trip. Readers explain the difference in several ways.
- Why the dust? The video: it treats the town like Gentile land. Chrysostom: a sign they took nothing from it, or a witness of the long journey made for its sake. Mark and Luke call it 'a testimony against them.'
- Only to Israel? This mission was to Israel (10:5-6; 15:24). After the resurrection the commission goes to all nations (28:19). Matthew holds both: Israel first, then the world.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Jews shook Gentile dust off their feet when returning home. Commentaries often say this, but the Gospels do not explain the gesture beyond 'a testimony against them' (Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5), so hold that background loosely.
- Five discourses do structure Matthew, but the link to the five books of the Torah is an interpretation; Matthew never states it, and 'every good Jew would have recognized' it cannot be shown.
- The quotation from Gary Smith's New American Commentary on Isaiah could not be checked here; read it in the commentary itself before repeating it.
- The link from 'freely give' to Isaiah 55 is the video's reading: Isaiah speaks of buying 'without money and without cost,' while Jesus speaks of receiving and giving 'freely.' The idea fits; the wording is not a quotation.
- The video reads from another English translation ('You received without paying, give without pay'); the LSB has 'Freely you received, freely give' (10:8).

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What is the difference between a disciple and an apostle? Which describes where you are right now?
2. If you had only the Old Testament, how would you explain 'the kingdom of heaven is at hand'?
3. Which of the passages (Psalm 2, Daniel 7, Jeremiah 23, Isaiah 55) helps you most to see Jesus as King?
4. What have you 'freely received'? Where is God asking you to give freely?
5. Do you ever trust yourself to accomplish God's mission instead of the God who sent you?
6. Where do you see the Father already at work around you this week?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: when God sends His people on a mission, He gives them everything they need to accomplish it. Not only food, supplies and shelter, but the very people who need to hear the message: 'inquire who is worthy.' The apostles did not have to make anyone worthy by their own great efforts; their job was to find those God had already prepared. The lesson is the same for us: if God sends us on a mission, He will give us everything we need. Sometimes we do not understand the mission in the moment, and sometimes we trust ourselves instead of the God who sent us. Jesus said, 'the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing' (John 5:19). This is the way to do ministry: recognize what the Father is already doing and go be a part of it.
- Study note (added): before you plan your next act of service, pray through Matthew 10:7-8. Write down one place you see the Father already at work (a person, a need, an open door), and one thing you have freely received that you can freely give there this week.
